_doc: Search performance budgets. `budgets` is the MEASURED record (npm run perf:search, live production data) and is documentation a human reads. `static` is the machine-enforced half: scripts/check-search-perf-budget.mjs (npm run ci:search-perf-budget) runs inside the secret-less ci:gates chain, so it cannot time a query — it enforces the structural invariants that keep the measured numbers true (ISR revalidate, fetch timeouts, cache wrappers, row caps, bounded reads). Refresh `budgets` with: npm run perf:search -- --json

measurement.environment: laptop over the public internet to Supabase project dwvlophlbvvygjfxcrhm, live production data. Vercel runs closer to the database, so production is faster than these numbers, never slower.
measurement.cacheNote: The measurement stubs next/cache so unstable_cache is a passthrough. Every timed call is a real query. 'cold' is the first run, 'warm' the median of the rest — a warm DATABASE, not a warm Next cache.
measurement.budgetRule: budgetMs is set at roughly 2x the worst observed cold time with a 500 ms floor, so network jitter and a cold Postgres buffer never trip it while a real regression (dropped index, lost cache wrapper, unbounded select) shows up as a multiple.

budgets.why: Whole-MV first page. The slowest unfiltered read, because no index narrows it before the sort.
The single most common search shape on the site. Indexed city read plus an exact count in one query.
City plus price plus beds. Adding registry filters must not cost more than the city read itself.
Ten filters across price, beds, baths, sqft, year, garage, acreage and two feature booleans, sorted by price. The all-filters sheet's worst realistic case.
PostGIS key resolution plus chunked .in() re-read. Two round trips by construction, so it carries the widest budget of the row paths.
Head count behind the live match total. Runs on every filter change, so it has to stay under a quarter second.
Same head count with seven predicates. The count must not diverge from the row read it labels.
3,808 facet rows paged out of search_facet_counts at 1,000 per page. Four round trips, cached for 15 minutes to match the table's refresh.
The shapes RPC on its own, one Bend-sized polygon returning 620 keys. Budget matches the drawn-shape row path it feeds.

knownDegraded.status: STILL DEGRADED, but for a DIFFERENT reason than before. The TOAST cause is closed; a second, independent, pre-existing cause is now the whole of it.
knownDegraded.finding: The harness shape is getListingsWithAdvanced({city:'Bend', statusFilter:'closed', hasView:true, limit:24}) and it still exhausts the 12s statement timeout (57014) with zero rows. Migrations 20260731210000 / 20260731212000 / 20260731220000 moved every details-reading predicate off listings.details onto two narrow trigger-maintained projections, which is measurably done: as the postgres role the same shape now returns real rows in 1,659-1,700 ms warm (6,225 ms cold) against 335,479 ms for the pre-change function on an identical interleaved run. What still fails is the ANON role, and it fails on a predicate this work never touched.
knownDegraded.remainingRootCause: ROW-LEVEL SECURITY plus a non-LEAKPROOF operator. public.listings has RLS enabled with `lower(coalesce("StandardStatus",'')) NOT LIKE 'coming%soon%'` for anon. PostgreSQL refuses to evaluate a non-leakproof user qual ahead of a security qual, and pg_catalog.texticlike (the ILIKE operator) has proleakproof = false. So for anon the planner cannot use idx_listings_city_trgm for `"City" ILIKE $1` and falls back to a Parallel Seq Scan of the 13 GB listings relation: 25.7 s of the 27.9 s total in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). The identical query as anon with a LEAKPROOF `"City" = 'Bend'` instead of ILIKE plans an Index Only Scan on idx_listings_city_status and finishes in 3.2 s, which isolates the cause exactly.
knownDegraded.provenPreExisting: This is not a regression from the flags work and is not specific to feature filters. As anon, closed+Bend with NO advanced filter at all measures 21,822 ms on the same RPC, versus 885-936 ms for the same call as postgres. Every anon call into search_listings_advanced that passes p_city pays it, which is the entire sold-search surface.
knownDegraded.whyNoBudgetAssigned: A budget would assert a completion time this path does not have. It stays here until the RLS/leakproof cause is closed.
knownDegraded.candidateRemedies: (1) Mark texticlike/texticnlike LEAKPROOF. One catalog change, fixes every RLS-protected ILIKE in the database, no semantics change to any query — but it is a database-wide security posture decision (a leaky operator can in principle disclose values of rows RLS is hiding), so it belongs to the broker, not to a perf fix. (2) Serve closed scopes from a materialized view the way on-market scopes already are (listing_search_mv), so the anon read never touches the RLS-protected base table. (3) Replace `"City" ILIKE p_city` with a leakproof equality — REJECTED: ILIKE 'Bend' also matches 'BEND', `lower()` is itself not leakproof (proleakproof = false), and MLS city casing is not canonical, so no equality rewrite is provably equivalent.
knownDegraded.whatTheFlagsProjectionFixed: Six feature predicates (hasView / hasPool / hasWaterfront / hasFireplace / hasOpenHouse / propertySubType) plus p_keywords no longer read listings.details at all. Measured as postgres, interleaved old vs new, 16 shapes: DEFECT-bend-closed-view 335,479 ms -> 25,430 ms under load and 1,659 ms warm on a settled instance; DEFECT-bend-closed-keywords 285,908 -> 13,745; redmond-closed-view+year sort 67,451 -> 5,040; sisters-closed-subtype-set 36,152 -> 3,045; sisters-multiflag+price_desc 17,464 -> 1,210; bend-active-keywords+price 112,436 -> 4,189. Isolated cost of the flags semi-join on closed+Bend: base 885-936 ms, with hasView 1,659-1,700 ms, i.e. about 770 ms.
knownDegraded.parity: 16 argument shapes, 2 interleaved passes, md5 fingerprint over (row order, ListNumber, ListingKey, ListPrice, ModificationTimestamp, md5(details)) plus full_count, compared against a byte-identical clone of the pre-change function. 14 shapes single-fingerprint. The 2 that differed (CTRL-bend-active-plain, CTRL-sisters-viewcontains) differ BY PASS and never by variant — old and new agree exactly within each pass; the change between passes is MLS drift on active listings over the 7 minutes between them.
knownDegraded.flagCorrectness: Whole-table, 594,190 rows, each flag compared against the RPC's own verbatim details expression: view 0, pool 0, waterfront 0, fireplace 0, open house 0, property sub-type 0, PublicRemarks 0 disagreements; 0 listings without a flags row and 0 without a remarks row.
knownDegraded.keywordVerdict: p_keywords moved to public.listing_remarks_search (273 MB heap) with a pg_trgm GIN index (243 MB, ~3.5 min build). The index cuts the keyword predicate's own evaluation from a 4,021 ms parallel seq scan over 34,995 blocks to a 1,037 ms bitmap scan over 27,952 blocks (the index probe itself is 262 ms), so it is kept. It does NOT make the shape reliable: keywords plus another filter on a large closed scope measures 1.7-20 s as postgres because the planner nested-loops 60,094 keyword matches into listings (25 s of a 26 s plan). That is a join-order problem, not a TOAST problem, and it is left open. Keyword-ONLY searches never reach this RPC — app/actions/listings.ts routes them to search_keyword_listings.

timeoutCeilings.name: withTimeout
timeoutCeilings.why: The split view degrades to an empty result rather than blocking the render on a slow Supabase.

timeoutCeilings.name: withTimeout
timeoutCeilings.why: Secondary fetches on the SEO search routes fail soft fast.

timeoutCeilings.name: LISTINGS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS
timeoutCeilings.why: Ceiling for the primary listings fetch. Raising it means a user waits longer on the known-degraded RPC path.

rowCaps.name: SHAPE_KEY_PAGE
rowCaps.why: One PostgREST page. Above 1,000 the response silently truncates.

rowCaps.name: MAX_SHAPE_KEYS
rowCaps.why: Ceiling on key resolution before the search degrades to the bbox fallback. Each 1,000 keys is another round trip.

rowCaps.name: SHAPE_KEY_CHUNK
rowCaps.why: Keys per .in() chunk. Larger chunks push the request URL past safe length.

rowCaps.name: PAGE_SIZE
rowCaps.why: Facet paging step, pinned to the PostgREST cap.

rowCaps.name: cap
rowCaps.why: Viewport row cap behind the map. Every row is a marker plus a card, so this is a render budget as much as a query budget.

rowCaps.name: limit
rowCaps.why: The filter schema's page-size ceiling. Above the PostgREST cap the read truncates without an error.
